Effect of thermal pretreatment and nanobubble 
addition water on methane production from cowpea hull 
anaerobic digestion
Christian Toochukwu Ogbonna1 · Delmaria Richards2 · Yabar Helmut3
Received: 25 July 2023 / Accepted: 15 October 2023 / Published online: 15 November 2023 
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2023
Abstract
Residual cowpea hull (CH) from akara (bean cake) processing constitutes a grow-
ing organic waste in countries with high production rates. CH has an unpleasant 
smell but rich in carbon, nitrogen, and micronutrients, which makes it a potential 
feedstock for energy recovery via anaerobic digestion (AD). However, the effect of 
the high antinutrient content, such as trypsin inhibitor (TI) previously reported in 
CH, and other parameters like moisture content on methane production need to be 
evaluated to promote its utilization as an AD feedstock. Anaerobic co-digestion of 
thermally pretreated cowpea hull and waste-activated sludge was investigated in this 
study, with a focus on the enhancing effect of thermal pretreatment (TP) at 83 and 
100% moisture content reduction (MCR) and nanobubble water (air and ­N2-NBW) 
addition on methane production. TP of CH under 100% MCR increased methane 
production by 12.9% compared to fresh CH. Additionally, replacing deionized water 
with ­N2-NBW further enhanced methane production by 20.9%. However, the effect 
of Air-NBW on methanogenesis was not significant. Improved CH biodegradability 
and the suppression of TI by TP may have facilitated the F/M interaction rate. How-
ever, the mechanisms of TI on microbial activity in an anaerobic digester need to be 
clarified. The electric power generating potential from the methane obtained in this

Introduction
Cowpea hull (CH) is becoming a critical environmental problem in the produc-
ing countries due to its high production rate and poor disposal practices [1, 2]. It 
is the seed coat of cowpea seed extract during cowpea/bean cake processing. The 
aggregate global production of cowpeas in 2019 was 9.8 million tons (MT) [3], rep-
resenting a 2.7-fold expansion since 2000. Nigeria and Niger account for 80% of 
global cowpea production. In 2011 and 2021, Nigeria produced 1.64 and 3.62 MT of 
cowpea seeds [4, 5]. The country’s growing waste management challenge has been 
extensively discussed [6], of which cowpea waste constitutes a significant portion 
[7]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) stands out among other organic waste treatment tech-
nologies due to its relative cost-effectiveness, clean energy source, and other nutri-
ent recovery [8–10].
AD of CH is a potential technique for organic waste disposal and biogas pro-
duction due to its wide availability in several countries [1, 11, 12] and the rich 
carbon and nitrogen content (18 to 25%), which is essential for AD system  [13, 
14]. Still, co-digestion with other nitrogen-rich substrates, such as waste-activated 
sludge (WAS), promotes process stability and nutritional balance [15] compared

to mono-digestion. Also, drying is imperative for CH AD to reduce its volume 
and weight for easy storage and transportation to the digester facility, it also 
improves the stinking odor and overall sanitation, especially among the rural pop-
ulation. Currently, limited studies have investigated the bio-gasification of CH. 
Biogas generation from cow dung, cowpea, and cassava peeling has been  was 
compared, and 67.9, 56.2, and 51.4% of methane content was obtained from each 
feedstock, respectively [16]. Recently, Co-digestion of CH with either WAS, or 
rice straw (RS)   showed an  increased total methane production by 18.95% or 
27.05%, correspondingly [2]. CH has also been investigated for glucose produc-
tion via a two-stage dilute-acid hydrolysis [7].
Various pretreatment options, such as mechanical, thermal, and biochemi-
cal, could enhance the AD of organic waste, such as CH. Several studies have 
revealed a positive effect of thermal pretreatment (TP) on the chemical compo-
sition of feedstock and biogas generation [17–19]. For example, TP of 180  °C 
on wheat straw observed a 53% increase in biogas generation [17]. The mecha-
nism for this effect is attributed to enhanced substrate solubility, which increases 
anaerobic biodegradability [20]. Moreover, several studies on CH for animal feed 
shows that it contains antinutritional factors such as trypsin inhibitors (TI) that 
counteract biochemical reactions [12, 21, 22]. In addition to improving solubi-
lization, TP is an effective technique to inactivate TI in legumes, breaking the 
intermolecular bonds in the complex structure of the TI [22, 23]. Also, combin-
ing thermal treatment with chemical addition could increase the efficiency of 
TI deactivation; sodium chloride (NaCl) has enhanced the deactivation of TI in 
soymilk by 74% [22]. However, chemical additions are costly and constitute a 
secondary pollution [24]. As a non-chemical-based catalyst, nanobubble water 
(NBW) has unique properties that enhance biogas production in AD. It is an envi-
ronmentally friendly, cost-effective technique for enhancing AD [25–28]. While 
past studies suggest that CH is feasible for biogas production, little is known 
about the influence of CH moisture content nor the effect of TI content on CH 
AD. Exploring these factors motivated this study. In other words, promoting CH 
as an attractive feedstock for biogas production requires addressing possible bot-
tlenecks that could impede its practical application for biogas production and 
optimizing the fermentation process for higher biogas production comparable to 
the conventional AD feedstock.
This study proposes a novel strategy to enhance methane production from CH. 
The hypothesis is that reducing the moisture content in CH via TP correlates with an 
enhanced AD process due to a reduced antinutrient content in CH. Second, restoring 
the dividend with NBW in place of deionized water (DW) would further enhance the 
hydrolysis process of CH. Therefore, the effect of different percentages of moisture 
content reduction (MCR) on biogas production and total solid reduction from CH 
co-digested with WAS was investigated, followed by the effect of adding different 
types of NBW (air- and nitrogen-NBW) in recompensing the removed organics from 
moisture reduction. Finally, the study estimates the potential electricity-generating 
capacity from the obtained methane production. To our knowledge, systematic stud-
ies on the effect of TP and NBW addition on CH anaerobic co-digestion are yet to be 
investigated in the literature. The findings will reveal the new technique to enhance

the  AD of CH for optimal biogas production and effective disposal methods for 
organic waste.
Materials and methods
Material collection and preparation
Cowpea seeds used in this study were purchased from a grocery shop in Tokyo, 
Japan. They were soaked in water at room temperature for 24 h to soften. The tender 
seeds were then manually peeled to separate the hull. The hull was dried under sun-
light and sealed in a plastic bag for the experiments. Digestate sludge was used as 
inoculum due to the high nitrogen and bacteria content. Digestate sludge and WAS 
were fetched from the Shimodate Wastewater Treatment Plant in Ibaraki Prefecture, 
Japan. To reduce the high liquid content, it was centrifuged at 4 °C, 9000 rpm for 
5 min, and stored at 4 °C before use for the batch experiment.
Thermal pretreatment and nanobubble water generation
The TP of CH was conducted in a laboratory drying oven (Yamato DX601) at 
105 °C temperature. Two MCRs (83.42 and 93.85) achieved during different reten-
tion times (3 and 48 h) were tested. NB. The two conditions were hereafter referred 
to as 83 and 100%MCR. The samples were cooled to room temperature, ground, 
and filtered through a 1 mm filter dish to increase the surface area and enhance the 
fermentation rate. NBW was generated using an ultra-fine bubble generator (HACK 
UFB, Japan), as shown in Fig. 1a, is the nanobubble generator. Air or ­N2 gas was 
injected into the bubble generator via the gas inlet (1), and 0.5 L of deionized water 
was connected to the water inlet (2). The pressure of the nanobubble generator was 
set at 0.24 MPa while gas and water flow rates were regulated at 0.6 L/h and 3 L/min

Batch anaerobic digestion setup
Two separate batch experiments were conducted to investigate the effects of TP 
and NBW addition on biogas production and total solid degradation. First, 1.5 g of 
CH was mixed with 0.5 g of WAS, a 3:1 optimum ratio obtained from our previous 
study [2]. The inoculum (digestate sewage sludge) was 1 g, all based on the VS con-
tent. The first batch experiment used CH at three conditions, as indicated in Table 1. 
Sample 1 had fresh CH as a control experiment (Untreated CH). In samples 2 and 
3, CH at 83% MCR (83%MCR) and 100% (100%MCR) were added, respectively. 
Deionized water (DW) was added to all samples to bring the working volume to 
60 mL. In the second batch, a replicate of the first batch, sample 3, was set up as the 
control experiment in sample 1. In samples 2 and 3, air-NBW (Air-NBW) or nitro-
gen-NBW ­(N2-NBW) was used to top the working volume instead of DW. All batch 
samples were fed into 100 mL serum glass bottles. The pH was carefully adjusted to 
7 ± 05 using a 2 M NaOH or HCL. The reactors were sealed with a silica gel stop-
per, and nitrogen gas was injected into the reactor for 2 min to purge air and ensure 
an anaerobic working condition before being placed into a mesophilic incubator at 
38 ± 1 °C. The experiments were conducted in duplicates, and the average results 
were reported (Table 2).

Analytical methods
The substrates were analyzed by the total solid (TS), volatile solid (VS), and mois-
ture content according to the standard method [30]. For the total organic carbon 
(TOC), nitrogen (TN), and Hydrogen (H) content, 3 g of dried CH were ground fil-
tered and sent to the elemental analysis center (University of Tsukuba, Japan). The 
dividend of TOC and TN gave the C/N ratio, while pH was measured with a pH 
meter (Mettler Toledo). For the cumulative biogas, gas volume was recorded every 
2 days by inserting a pressure-tight glass syringe into the reactor via the soft silicate 
cap. Afterward, 1 mL of the gas was analyzed in gas chromatography (GC-8A, Shi-
madzu, Japan) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (80 °C) and Porapak Q 
column (60 °C) and ­N2 as carrier gas for the methane, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen 
content. The methane production was obtained by multiplying methane content by 
the total gas produced [2]. Although the inoculum’s gas output was not accounted 
for in the net gas production, it had been cultivated for 14 days, and gas was released 
before use.
Quantification of potential electrical energy
Nigeria and Niger Republic produce over 80% of global cowpea production annually 
[31]. Approximately 3.6 million tons of cowpea are consumed annually in Nigeria, 
mainly for preparing bean flour and bean cake dishes such as moi-moi and akara 
[32]. The study acknowledges that abiotic and biotic stresses, cultivation methods, 
and socioeconomic constraints influence cowpea production. These limitations can 
impact the overall availability of CH as a potential feedstock. Consequently, these 
factors must be considered in understanding the feasibility of CH’s production of 
biogas [11, 33]. However, the abundant nature of WAS and NBW is assumed to be 
available for co-digestion with CH. Therefore, it is contingent on sludge production 
from municipal and industrial sewage plants and NBW commercially produced from 
a nanobubble generator. The calculation utilizes Nigeria’s 2020 output of 3.65 MT 
cowpea gross production as a case study to estimate the electrical energy generation 
potential. The results are calculated by quantifying the crop residue generation, col-
lection factor, surplus availability, residue dryness factor, the ratio of volatile solids, 
and biogas generation rate [34]. After dehulling, 1 kg of cowpea seed gave 124.20 g 
of CH used in the computation for waste-to-energy reprocessing. Equations 1 and 2 
determine the potential electrical energy from fresh and pretreated CH AD.

Results and discussion
The effect of CH at two different TP (83 and 100% MCR) and two different NBW 
addition (air and ­N2-NBW) was investigated in wet mesophilic anaerobic co-diges-
tion with WAS for optimizing biogas production and total solid degradation. The 
initial pH was 7.0, and the working temperature was controlled at 38 ℃. The AD 
duration was 16 days.
Characteristics of the feedstock
The physicochemical characteristics of feedstock are determined for their possible 
influence on the stability and efficiency in the batch experiment. Table 3 shows the 
characteristics of CH, WAS, and inoculum used in this study. Notably, CH has a 
total solid content of 92%, of which volatile solid accounts for 96.45%, implying a 
highly degradable portion that could be exploited for biogas production. Although 
WAS has a lower TS (48%), the volatile solids per TS is also high (95.46%). The 
high nitrogen content in WAS (6.8%) has been used to compensate for the low nitro-
gen content in rice straw (0.9%) co-digestion [35]. The carbon content in CH is 
44.84 wt%, while the nitrogen content is 2.2 wt%, implying a C/N ratio of 20.02. 
Compared to 1.5 wt% of nitrogen in cowpea seed [36], CH is more rich in nitrogen.
Effect of thermal pretreatment on biogas and methane production
The effect of TP was investigated to enhance the efficiency of AD of CH and WAS 
using digestate sludge as inoculum. TP is expected to improve the solubility of CH, 
breaking the rigid cell wall structure that prevents organic matter digestibility dur-
ing the AD of lignocellulosic materials. In doing so, the activity of the high antinu-
trient content in CH, such as trypsin inhibitor (TI), could equally be reduced. The

efficiency of AD in this study is evaluated by the increase in the cumulative biogas, 
methane production and the total solid degradation (discussed separately). Figure 2 
shows the biogas production from the co-digestion of CH.
A significant increase in biogas production was achieved by TP at 100% MCR, 
i.e., 219.14 mL/g VS, followed by 83% MCR (217.02 mL/g VS). Compared to fresh 
CH (197.93 mL/g VS), this is a 10.7 and 9.6% increase in total biogas production. 
The result implies that increasing the MCR in CH achieved by the longer retention 
time of TP resulted in enhanced anaerobic digestion. The daily biogas trend shows 
that all samples produced an equal amount of biogas on the first day (Fig. 2). How-
ever, the untreated CH had accumulated more biogas on day 2 (70 mL) compared 
to 100% MCR (60 mL). By day 4, the CH at 100% MCR and 83% MCR exceeded 
the untreated CH, and the trend was sustained until the end of fermentation on 
day 16, when biogas production dropped to less than 1.0 mL/day. The cumulative 
methane production followed a similar trend as the biogas production. TP at 83 and 
100%MCR produced more methane at 116.15 and 114.41 mL/g VS, respectively, 
compared to fresh CH (104.26 mL/g VS).
TP improves the substrate solubilization in an AD system [20]. It disintegrates 
cell walls and facilitates the release of intracellular matter into the aqueous phase, 
which augments biodegradability, thus improving AD with lower retention time and 
higher biogas generation [37, 38]. It also increases WAS AD’s microbial popula-
tions and biogas yield, yielding the highest biogas rate of 0.42 L/g−1 volatile solid 
(VS) [18]. Although the result obtained in this study is significant, the increase in 
biogas and methane production due to TP was lower than those reported in the lit-
erature utilizing the same pretreatment method. For example, Coffee husk TP at 120 
and 180 °C resulted in a 7.64 and 8.98 g TOC/L increase in organic compounds 
solubilization, respectively [20]. Pineapple peel waste in a batch AD system showed 
enhanced biogas generation and decreased AD process lag time, resulting in the 
highest biogas production volume of 616.33 mL (357.190 mL/g VS) [19].
Regarding the more biogas production from fresh CH at the start of the fermenta-
tion (Fig. 2), this could be attributed to the high galactooligosaccharides content in

CH, which exhibits quick fermentation under anaerobic conditions [39]. However, 
the biogas potential was unsustainable and steadily decreased when other antinu-
trients began to degrade in subsequent days. Dehulling cowpea seeds has shown a 
30.25% and 26.80% reduction of raffinose and stachyose (galactooligosaccharides 
types) [40], confirming that a significant portion of both probiotics and antinutrients 
remains on CH. Although the significant enhancement in substrate AD degradation, 
evident in the biogas and methane production, could be attributed to the increased 
solubility. Several studies on CH’s nutritional characteristics for animal feed indicate 
a high content of antinutrients such as TI. A total of 7.52 U/mg of TI activity in raw 
cowpea has been reported [41]. Trypsin enhances methane production, facilitating 
hydrolysis and acetic acid conversion during the AD of WAS [42]. On the contrary, 
TI reduces the activation and catabolism of proteins [43], including the digestion of 
proteins [22]. It is assumed in this study that at no pretreatment, fresh CH having 
a high content of TI resulted in a decrease in methane production due to repressed 
microbial activities in the AD system. Hence, microbial analysis of CH before and 
after TP is recommended as a prerequisite step in further study on CH AD to ascer-
tain the effect of TI.
Effect of nanobubble water addition on biogas and methane production
In the second batch experiment, the Cowpea hull at 100 percent MCR was used 
to investigate the synergistic effect of TP and NBW addition on CH AD. Figure 3 
shows the effect of different NBW types (Air and nitrogen) on  daily biogas and 
cumulative  methane production after 16  days of batch retention time. The daily 
biogas production (Fig. 3a) shows that biogas production was over 30 mL/day in all 
setups on day 1, while the peak biogas production was recorded on day 3. The biogas 
production on day 3 was 59.06, 60.11, and 64.51 for CH at 100% MCR, Air-NBW, 
and ­N2-NBW addition. On the other hand, the cumulative methane production was 
116.15, 116.83, and 129 mL/g VS for CH at 100% MCR, Air-NBW, and ­N2-NBW

addition, respectively (Fig. 3b). Nitrogen-NBW significantly enhanced methane pro-
duction by 11.35% compared to CH without NBW. However, methane production 
was only slightly improved (0.59%) when air-NBW was used. While ­N2-NBW had a 
relatively similar enhancement in biogas production (10.5%), Air-NBW, on the other 
hand, enhanced total biogas production by threefold (2.5%) compared to methane 
production.
Microbial activities in water treatment and fermentation of human excrement 
have been enhanced with NBW addition [26]. Although significant, the enhancing 
effect of NBW recorded in this study is relatively low compared to previous studies. 
A 29% increase in methane production was achieved in WAS single digestion when 
­N2-NBW was added, with no noticeable change in methane content. [27]. A 39% 
increase in cumulative methane production was obtained when ­N2-NBW was added 
to pig manure due to enhanced hydrolysis [44]. Similarly, a follow-up investigation 
showed a 25.0% increase from the same substrate under high solids (3–6% TS)[45]. 
The highest cumulative methane production (132.16 mL g VS) was achieved when 
NBW was added to corn straw AD [28]. Nitrogen-NBW promoted seed germination 
rate by 25% compared to water, while no significant effect was seen with air or car-
bon dioxide-NBW [46]. Methanogenic activity is sensitive to different environments 
[47] and may have been altered by antinutrients in CH that could not be removed 
entirely by TP.
Another assumption for the relatively low enhancing effect of NBW in this study 
is that NBW may have rapidly decomposed in the reactor during the 16 days of fer-
mentation. On the contrary, a study showed that ­N2, ­O2, Ar, and air-NBW prepared 
under an aqueous solution lasted over 60 days [48]. However, they also found that 
­CO2 was unstable in water and lasted only 5 days [48]. NBW used in this study 
may not have been fully formed due to technical errors during the bubble genera-
tion, leading to short stability in the reactor. Recall that the retention time for the 
NBW was 5 min less than the recommended 30 min in previous studies [27, 29]. 
This assumption also explains the lower enhancement from air-NBW compared to 
­N2-NBW, as decomposed air-NBW will rapidly oxidize the anaerobic working con-
dition compared to ­N2-NBW.
Overall, our findings revealed that NBW has a different effect on hydrolysis and 
methanogenesis based on the type of NBW and the reacting substrate. However, 
there tends to be a consensus on the positive enhancing effect of NBW on AD sys-
tems in the literature. This study, therefore, recommends analyzing the characteris-
tics of the generated NBW, such as the mobility and zeta potential, before the AD 
batch experiment to ascertain the stability of the bubbles. And at the same time, tak-
ing a careful consideration of the targeted substrates characteristics.
While successful optimization of AD following the direct addition of different 
chemicals and complex enzymes such as carbohydrolases, peptidases, and lipases 
has been reported [37]. NBW comprises cheap gasses with the potential to improve 
the anaerobic condition of the methanogen [29]. NBW had a positive effect in this 
study, particularly nitrogen-NBW enhanced hydrolysis, and methanogenesis in the 
AD of CH. Requiring only the initial cost for the bubble generator and the inexpen-
sive nitrogen and air gases, NBW is a relatively cheap and environmentally friendly 
technology compared to other optimization options. Hence, NBW-supplemented AD

The pH trend and total organic solid decomposition
After 16 days of mesophilic anaerobic digestion with initial pH adjusted to 7 ± 05. 
The pH trend of all the samples remained within 6.8–7.0. Fresh CH, 83% MCR, 
100% MCR, Air-NBW, and ­N2-NBW had a final pH values of 6.90, 6.87, 6.85, 6.84, 
and 6.89, respectively (Fig. 4), affirming that methanogens generally survive in a 
neutral pH (7) conditions to biodegrade the feedstock [49]. The most stable pH trend 
was found in ­N2-NBW, having the lowest acidification rate (6.84), Similarly, Hes-
born et al. [50] achieved the same pH trend (6.8) when the initial alkalinity of the 
digester was increased by 6000 g/L compared to unadjusted alkalinity. On the con-
trary, another study found that acid formers could be best controlled at a pH of 6 
for the bioconversion of citrus waste [51]. Notwithstanding, the relatively stable pH 
in all reactors conforms with the successful fermentation of CH and WAS within 
16 days of batch retention time, achieving a high average methane percentage (70%) 
in all test groups. A customarily operated AD system produces biogas with methane 
content ranging from 55 to 70% [52]. This implies that optimum working pH condi-
tion was maintained [53].
The total and volatile solid reduction is not only an effective indicator of the effi-
ciency of the AD performance in this study. It is considered essential as an organic 
waste disposal technique. Figure 5 shows the total solid and volatile solid reduc-
tion after the AD. All seven batch setups had a similar total solid and volatile solid 
reduction trend. The total solid reduction was 34% in all reactors except for Air-
NBW, which had a 32.5% TS reduction. Correspondingly, the volatile solid reduc-
tion was 44% in Air-NBW, 45% with no NBW addition (100% MCR), and slightly 
above 45% in other batch reactors. Although lignins are difficult to degrade, our

Electrical energy generation
The theoretical electrical energy potential is derived from feedstock utilized in the 
experiment and computation contingent on Nigeria’s production of CH and decor-
ticating for food preparation. Thus, the results are amenable. The computation used 
the average daily methane production (Table 3). The result reveals that the poten-
tial biogas of 47.13 and 68.90 million ­m3 generated by co-fermentation of untreated 
and thermally treated CH with WAS under anaerobic conditions can be converted to 
50.96 − 75.36 GWh. Furthermore, it addresses the ability to reduce carbon-based 
electrical energy, which constituted 77% of the 27,042 GWh electricity generated in 
2020 [55].
Consequently, 0.19 to 0.27% of the total electricity capacity generated in 2020 
could be replaced by the energy recovered from waste substrates utilized in the 
experiment. Besides, biogas could be used as cooking fuel, especially in Nigeria’s 
remote areas, where households depend primarily on traditional biomass and kero-
sene [56]. The green energy generated can aid in mitigating methane emissions by 
recycling organic waste that would otherwise escape to the atmosphere from open 
dump landfilling, which is common in Nigeria [57]. The synergistic benefit of AD

Conclusion
Methane production and organic solid reduction rate from cowpea hull co-
digested with waste-activated sludge were enhanced by thermal pretreatment and 
­N2-nanobubble water addition, increasing methane production by 12.9 and 20.9%, 
respectively, compared to fresh cowpea hull. However, no significant effect was 
observed with Air-NBW. This result can be attributed to the improved substrate’s 
digestibility and deactivation of antinutrients, which facilitated the F/M interaction 
rate. The suppression of trypsin inhibitors may have aided the AD process, but the 
mechanisms in anaerobic microbial activity need to be clarified. The results reveal 
that 47.13 to 68.90 million ­m3 of biogas generated by co-fermentation of untreated 
and thermally treated cowpea hull with WAS can be converted to 75.36 GWh, which 
displaces 0.27% of the total fossil fuel-based electricity capacity generated in 2020. 
Besides, the green energy generated can mitigate methane emissions by recycling 
organic waste that would otherwise be landfilled.
